Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i first visited the allotments behind the old bus garage in april 2022, after my neighbor mara said the committee had one narrow plot left. from the pavement it looked less like a garden than a collection of fences, wheelbarrows and sheds, with the flats on glen street rising behind it. i was living alone then, and my kitchen window faced a brick wall, so the thought of having soil outside felt unusually generous. mara showed me the path and said, “the key is not to plan the whole year on your first day.” i nodded like i understood, although i had already brought a notebook with a planting calendar in it.

my plot was number 18, about four metres by six, with a broken paving slab near the gate and a thick patch of couch grass at the back. the previous tenant had left two black buckets, a rusted fork and a label that said “red onions,” though there were no onions in the ground. i spent the first saturday pulling weeds and putting them in a blue compost sack, then learned from the site steward, leon, that couch grass should not go in the regular compost because it can grow again. i had not thought about weeds having this kind of future. leon lent me a garden fork and showed me how to loosen the soil without turning every layer upside down.

1. the first thing i planted was lettuce, mostly because the seed packet said it was easy. i sowed the seeds too close together, and by may there was a green, crowded row that looked healthy from the path but was difficult to thin without feeling wasteful. mara told me to leave a hand’s width between the plants. “they need room to become the thing you wanted,” she said. i took the small lettuce leaves home and put them in sandwiches with mustard. the taste was sharper than the supermarket kind, though that could have been because i was pleased with myself.

2. in june, i tried beans on a cane frame that i tied together with garden twine. the frame leaned after the first windy night, and one cane caught against the fence, so i rebuilt it with four extra canes that leon had in his shed. across the path, a retired teacher called mr patel grew runner beans in a neat double row and gave me advice without making it sound like a lesson. he said the flowers would bring bees, and that i should check beneath the leaves because the pods hide there. the first time i found a pod, it was long and slightly curved, and i called mara over as if i had discovered something rare. she laughed, but she came to look.

3. the plot also taught me that growing food is not a steady sequence of successes. in july, the courgette leaves developed pale patches, and i worried it was a disease. leon looked at them and said it might be powdery mildew, which often shows up when the weather is dry. i watered at the base of the plant in the evening and removed two badly marked leaves, but i did not know whether that would make much difference. meanwhile, pigeons pulled up three young beetroot seedlings. i covered the remaining row with green mesh and used two bricks to hold it down. the mesh looked clumsy, but the beetroot stayed in place.

the site had its own rhythms besides the plants. on tuesday evenings, people often arrived after work with their bags still over one shoulder, and on sunday mornings there was usually a small queue for the shared tap. a hand-painted notice on the shed door asked everyone to turn it off properly, because it dripped into a puddle that spread under the shelves. one week, someone left a bowl of plums on the table with a note saying, “take some, they’re all ripe at once.” i took four, and left a jar of mint tea bags in return. nobody discussed the exchange, but the bowl and the tea bags kept appearing through the summer.

by august, the narrow strip beside my fence had become useful for things i had not planned to grow. a volunteer sunflower had come up near the compost bin, and its head was almost level with the shed roof. i did not know who had planted it, so i asked around; nobody claimed it. i left it there, partly because the bees visited it and partly because it made the plot easier to find from the entrance. under it, i grew radishes in a shallow tray. they came out small and peppery, and i ate them on the path while talking to mr patel about the rain forecast.

i kept the notebook, but the planting calendar slowly turned into a record of other things: when the tap was repaired, which gate stuck in wet weather, and the day mara brought a thermos of coffee because she knew i had arrived before breakfast. i wrote down that the first beans weighed 430 grams, and that the lettuce was finished by the second week of june. i also wrote, “ask before borrowing the blue watering can,” after i carried it to my plot and discovered it belonged to the people at number 11. they were kind about it, and i returned it the same afternoon.

in october, i cleared the bean vines and put the dry stems beside the compost bays. the plot looked exposed again, with the soil showing between the paths and the sunflower head turned brown. i still had a few beetroot in the ground, and i was unsure whether they would grow much larger before the cold weather. i left them for another fortnight and checked after the first frost. they were firm enough to pull, though two had split. walking home with soil on my gloves, i thought about mara’s advice from that first day. i had not planned the whole year, and the notebook was no longer a schedule; it was a collection of small observations about a place and the people who used it. i was glad i had the plot, even in the months when it was mostly bare.", "output": "I first visited the allotments behind the old bus garage in April 2022, after my neighbor Mara said the committee had one narrow plot left. From the pavement, it looked less like a garden than a collection of fences, wheelbarrows, and sheds, with the flats on Glen Street rising behind it. I was living alone then, and my kitchen window faced a brick wall, so the thought of having soil outside felt unusually generous. Mara showed me the path and said, “The key is not to plan the whole year on your first day.” I nodded as if I understood, although I had already brought a notebook with a planting calendar in it.

My plot was number 18, about four metres by six, with a broken paving slab near the gate and a thick patch of couch grass at the back. The previous tenant had left two black buckets, a rusted fork, and a label that said “red onions,” though there were no onions in the ground. I spent the first Saturday pulling weeds and putting them in a blue compost sack. Then I learned from the site steward, Leon, that couch grass should not go in the regular compost because it can grow again. I had not thought about weeds having that kind of future. Leon lent me a garden fork and showed me how to loosen the soil without turning every layer upside down.

1. The first thing I planted was lettuce, mostly because the seed packet said it was easy. I sowed the seeds too close together, and by May there was a green, crowded row that looked healthy from the path but was difficult to thin without feeling wasteful. Mara told me to leave a hand’s width between the plants. “They need room to become the thing you wanted,” she said. I took the small lettuce leaves home and put them in sandwiches with mustard. They tasted sharper than the supermarket kind, though that may have been because I was pleased with myself.

2. In June, I tried beans on a cane frame that I tied together with garden twine. The frame leaned after the first windy night, and one cane caught against the fence, so I rebuilt it with four extra canes that Leon had in his shed. Across the path, a retired teacher called Mr Patel grew runner beans in a neat double row and gave me advice without making it sound like a lesson. He said the flowers would bring bees and that I should check beneath the leaves because the pods hide there. The first time I found a pod, it was long and slightly curved. I called Mara over as if I had discovered something rare. She laughed, but came to look.

3. The plot also taught me that growing food is not a steady sequence of successes. In July, the courgette leaves developed pale patches, and I worried it was a disease. Leon looked at them and said it might be powdery mildew, which often shows up when the weather is dry. I watered at the base of the plant in the evening and removed two badly marked leaves, but I did not know whether that would make much difference. Meanwhile, pigeons pulled up three young beetroot seedlings. I covered the remaining row with green mesh and used two bricks to hold it down. The mesh looked clumsy, but the beetroot stayed in place.

The site had its own rhythms besides those of the plants. On Tuesday evenings, people often arrived after work with their bags still over one shoulder, and on Sunday mornings there was usually a small queue for the shared tap. A hand-painted notice on the shed door asked everyone to turn it off properly because it dripped into a puddle that spread beneath the shelves. One week, someone left a bowl of plums on the table with a note saying, “Take some, they’re all ripe at once.” I took four and left a jar of mint tea bags in return. Nobody discussed the exchange, but the bowl and the tea bags kept appearing through the summer.

By August, the narrow strip beside my fence had become useful for things I had not planned to grow. A volunteer sunflower had come up near the compost bin, and its head was almost level with the shed roof. I did not know who had planted it, so I asked around; nobody claimed it. I left it there, partly because the bees visited it and partly because it made the plot easier to find from the entrance. Under it, I grew radishes in a shallow tray. They came out small and peppery, and I ate them on the path while talking to Mr Patel about the rain forecast.

I kept the notebook, but the planting calendar slowly turned into a record of other things: when the tap was repaired, which gate stuck in wet weather, and the day Mara brought a thermos of coffee because she knew I had arrived before breakfast. I wrote down that the first beans weighed 430 grams and that the lettuce was finished by the second week of June. I also wrote, “Ask before borrowing the blue watering can,” after I carried it to my plot and discovered it belonged to the people at number 11. They were kind about it, and I returned it that same afternoon.

In October, I cleared the bean vines and put the dry stems beside the compost bays. The plot looked exposed again, with the soil showing between the paths and the sunflower head turned brown. I still had a few beetroot in the ground, and I was unsure whether they would grow much larger before the cold weather. I left them for another fortnight and checked after the first frost. They were firm enough to pull, though two had split. Walking home with soil on my gloves, I thought about Mara’s advice from that first day. I had not planned the whole year, and the notebook was no longer a schedule; it was a collection of small observations about a place and the people who used it. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i visited willow bend allotments on three saturday mornings in may, first with a friend who already rents a plot and then twice on my own. i am reviewing it as a visitor, not as someone who has rented a bed there, so i can describe what i saw but not how the waiting list or the growing season works over time. the site is on the edge of a housing estate, behind a low brick wall and a green metal gate. from the pavement it looks small, but the paths open into more rows than i expected.

The gate was open during both of my solo visits, and there was a paper notice asking visitors to close it behind them. The notice also said dogs should be kept on leads. I saw one dog, with its owner, and it stayed on the main path. There is a narrow paved strip from the gate to the first beds, then the paths are mostly packed soil and gravel. After rain, two low sections were muddy, though I could get around them without stepping into anyone's plot. The route is not fully level, and the gravel shifts underfoot in places. I would not describe the whole site as easy to get around if you use a wheelchair or have trouble walking.

The plots vary a lot in size and in how they are used. Some are tidy rectangles with labeled rows, while others have flowers around the edges and vegetables mixed together. I saw beans climbing netting, broad leaves that my friend identified as squash, and several small greenhouses. One plot had a painted sign saying “please leave the comfrey alone,” which made me smile, although I did not know what the plant was until my friend explained it. A few beds looked newly cleared, and one had a pile of old canes beside it. I could not tell whether those things meant the owners were behind on work or simply preparing for the next planting.

My friend showed me the shared shed, which is near the middle of the site. It had a combination lock, and she let me see inside while she returned a hand fork. There were several spades, watering cans and wheelbarrows, but I did not count them or check their condition closely. A handwritten card on the door said, “Please put tools back clean and tell us if anything breaks.” My friend said people generally do this, but that is her experience, not something I can verify from three visits. I liked that there were shared tools, though I would want to know how access works before relying on them for a plot.

1. A few practical things I noticed: there is a tap beside the shed, a compost bay at the far end, and a small table with a box for seed swaps. The tap had a short hose attached when I visited. The compost bay had a sign asking people not to put in cooked food or plastic, and there were separate heaps that appeared to be at different stages. The seed box was mostly packets in paper envelopes, with a note saying to write the variety and year on anything left there. I did not take seeds. The table also had a printed sheet advertising a Saturday morning tool-repair session, but the date on it had already passed, so I cannot say whether those sessions are still happening.

The people I met were friendly without making the site feel like a public attraction. On my first visit, a woman watering nearby pointed out the path to the shed when she saw us looking around. She said, “It’s all right to have a look, just don’t pick anything.” That was clear and reasonable. On the next visit I had a brief chat with a man who was tying up raspberry canes; he said the allotments had been there longer than the flats across the road. I did not ask him for a date, so I am not treating that as a precise history. Nobody offered a formal tour, and there was no map at the gate when I went.

The site has a few comforts, but it is basic. I saw a covered bench beside the noticeboard and a rain barrel behind the shed. There is no café or shop, and I did not see a public toilet. The noticeboard had information about plot rules, a local gardening group and a notice seeking spare plant pots. Some papers were curling at the corners, and one small notice was partly hidden under another. The main gate and paths were easy enough to find from the street, but the address was not obvious from the pavement; I used my friend’s directions the first time. It is quiet once you are inside, although traffic is audible over the wall.

Overall, I enjoyed looking around Willow Bend, especially the mix of productive beds and flowers and the visible sharing of tools and seeds. It feels like a working allotment rather than a landscaped garden, which is part of its appeal to me. The muddy stretches, uneven routes and lack of visitor facilities are real limitations, and my visits do not tell me what it is like to rent a plot there. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "Common Thread Laundry Cooperative: spring hours and service update

Common Thread Laundry Cooperative will begin its spring schedule on Monday, April 7. The public laundry room at 1840 Alder Street will be open from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. every day, with the last wash accepted at 7:45 p.m. The staffed service desk will be open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Saturday and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Sunday. Members may continue using their entry cards outside desk hours. The schedule will remain in place through September 28.

The cooperative has added two 40-pound front-loading washers and one folding table near the west wall. The new machines are available to members and walk-in customers at the same posted rates as the existing large washers. Each load still requires a separate cycle payment, and the machines do not accept cash. Customers can pay with a member card or the reloadable laundry card sold at the desk. “We wanted a little more room for bedding and shared household loads,” said operations lead Marisol Vega. “The new washers give people another option during the busiest part of the week.”

A technician inspected the dryers on March 26 and replaced the belt on dryer 12. All 18 dryers are currently available. The lint bins are beside the machines, and customers are asked to clear the screen after each load. The cooperative has also moved the spare laundry carts to the marked area beside the front entrance. Carts should be returned there after use so that the accessible aisle between the folding tables remains clear.

The board will hold its monthly member meeting in the upstairs room on Thursday, April 10, at 6:30 p.m. The meeting is open to cooperative members, and a remote access link will be sent to members who request one by noon that day. The agenda includes a review of the spring schedule, a report on equipment repairs, and a discussion of the proposed shared-supply cabinet. No change to the current detergent policy is on the agenda. Members may send questions to the desk before the meeting; staff will add them to the meeting packet when received by Wednesday afternoon.

For customers using the wash-and-fold service, the regular intake window is 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Saturday. Orders are weighed at drop-off, and the receipt lists the estimated pickup day. The usual turnaround is two business days, but orders received after 3 p.m. are recorded on the next service day. Bedding is accepted if it fits in the marked blue bags. The service does not include dry cleaning, stain removal guarantees, or same-day pickup. “Please tell us if a bag contains items that need to be kept together,” said desk coordinator Eli Brooks. “We can attach a note to the order, though we cannot promise that every item will finish in the same load.”

1. Spring schedule and service details
   - Public laundry room: 7 a.m.–9 p.m. daily; last wash accepted at 7:45 p.m.
   - Service desk: 8 a.m.–6 p.m. Monday–Saturday; 10 a.m.–4 p.m. Sunday.
   - Wash-and-fold intake: 9 a.m.–3 p.m. Monday–Saturday.
   - Member cards remain active outside staffed desk hours.
   - Current machine rates and detergent rules are unchanged.

The cooperative’s posted rates remain $3.25 for a standard washer, $5.50 for a large washer, and $0.25 for each six minutes of dryer time. The new 40-pound washers use the large-washer rate. The service desk can reload laundry cards in increments of $5, $10, or $20, and card balances do not expire. A printed rate sheet is posted beside the payment station and is available in large type at the desk. Customers who find an incorrect charge can bring the receipt to staff during desk hours for review.

The shared-supply cabinet is a proposal for the April 10 meeting, not a current service. The draft plan would allow members to leave unopened laundry supplies for other members to use, with a labeled shelf for fragrance-free products.
